builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Game-Theoretic Solvers with Bayesian Opponent Modeling and Moral Rhetoric Framing for GLEE
summary: Replaces end-to-end learned or purely LLM-prompted negotiation and persuasion policies with a hybrid stack: classical solvers (Rubinstein, Faratin, Kamenica-Gentzkow) for numeric moves, an online Bayesian layer estimating hidden opponent parameters, a Thompson-sampling bandit over five moral-foundation framings, and an LLM only for message generation. Costs are modest in compute but high in engineering complexity: solver implementations per game type, opponent-model maintenance, bandit tuning, and the guardrails the authors report needing because theoretically optimal policies fail in live settings. After adoption, the main risks are misspecified opponent archetypes, bandit misallocation on short interactions, correlation-not-causation in the rhetoric result, and degraded play against opponents outside the modeled pool.
rationale: The approach runs on constrained infrastructure and is credible for teams shipping negotiation or persuasion features, but its live-setting failure modes and correlational evidence require workload-specific validation before adoption.
technique: Game-theoretic solver with Bayesian opponent modeling and rhetoric framing

claims.statement: Replaces end-to-end learned or purely LLM-prompted negotiation and persuasion policies with a hybrid stack: classical solvers (Rubinstein, Faratin, Kamenica-Gentzkow) for numeric moves, an online Bayesian layer estimating hidden opponent parameters, a Thompson-sampling bandit over five moral-foundation framings, and an LLM only for message generation. Costs are modest in compute but high in engineering complexity: solver implementations per game type, opponent-model maintenance, bandit tuning, and the guardrails the authors report needing because theoretically optimal policies fail in live settings. After adoption, the main risks are misspecified opponent archetypes, bandit misallocation on short interactions, correlation-not-causation in the rhetoric result, and degraded play against opponents outside the modeled pool.

No multiplicative performance factor is reported; the strongest result is correlational: moral-rhetoric framing in persuasion games was strongly associated with buyer purchases (chi^2=616.7, p approximately 3.7e-132) across 9,337 live-game messages, surviving controls, plus a 13,200-game Monte Carlo evaluation against 11 synthetic archetypes.
